lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion of Mars and Outer Planets
top_level_objectives: Describe how Mars appears to move against background stars over weeks and identify the retrograde loop.
Explain why retrograde motion is only apparent and results from relative motion between Earth and an outer planet.
Compare geocentric and heliocentric interpretations of retrograde motion.
Relate the size and timing of retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn to their orbital distances and speeds.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the observational puzzle by showing Mars’s usual eastward drift and its temporary reversal against the stars.
key_visuals: A nighttime sky dome with constellations as a fixed background
Mars positions marked across multiple nights
A traced path showing eastward motion, slowdown, westward loop, and return to eastward motion
student_actions: Step through observations night by night
Identify where Mars slows, reverses direction, and resumes normal motion
Describe the loop as seen from Earth’s surface

scenes.brief_purpose: Help students characterize the timing and shape of retrograde motion as an observed pattern.
key_visuals: A compressed timeline of several months of Mars positions
Highlighted stationary points before and after the loop
Direction arrows showing eastward and westward apparent motion
student_actions: Mark the two stationary points
Estimate how long the retrograde interval lasts compared with normal drift
Summarize the observed pattern in short prose

scenes.scene_name: Why the Observation Was a Historical Problem
scenes.brief_purpose: Show why retrograde motion challenged simple geocentric expectations and motivated alternative models.
key_visuals: Earth-centered view with Mars on a deferent and epicycle
A side-by-side contrast between a simple circular geocentric path and the added epicycle construction
Annotations emphasizing that the loop must be built into the model
student_actions: Inspect how an epicycle reproduces the observed loop
State what is awkward or less intuitive about this explanation
Connect the observation to the historical model debate

scenes.scene_name: Heliocentric View from Outside the Solar System
scenes.brief_purpose: Reveal that Earth and Mars both move smoothly around the Sun and that no planet actually reverses its orbit.
key_visuals: Top-down solar system view with the Sun, Earth’s inner orbit, and Mars’s outer orbit
Earth moving faster than Mars
Motion trails showing both planets continuing in the same orbital direction
student_actions: Follow Earth and Mars through their orbits
Verify that neither planet physically turns around
Note the interval when Earth is catching up to and passing Mars

scenes.brief_purpose: Link the outside orbital view to the apparent loop seen from Earth and explain retrograde as a line-of-sight effect.
key_visuals: Simultaneous split view: sky path of Mars and top-down heliocentric motion
A sightline drawn from Earth to Mars across several dates
An analogy panel showing one car appearing to drift backward as another passes
student_actions: Advance the same dates in both views together
Observe how the sightline shift maps onto the retrograde loop
Explain in their own words why Mars only appears to move backward

scenes.scene_name: Comparing Mars with Jupiter and Saturn
scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the concept by comparing how other outer planets show retrograde loops of different apparent sizes.
key_visuals: Overlaid apparent sky tracks for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
A top-down comparison of Earth overtaking each planet at different relative speeds and distances
Labels indicating that farther planets show smaller, less dramatic loops
student_actions: Compare the width and curvature of the three loops
Relate loop size to orbital distance and relative motion
Identify which planet shows the most dramatic retrograde and justify the choice

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate learning by having students predict when retrograde should occur and what conditions produce it.
key_visuals: A simplified orbital diagram with Earth approaching, aligned with, and moving past Mars
A blank or partially completed apparent sky path for students to interpret
Key takeaways summarizing observation, model, and cause
student_actions: Predict the orbital configuration that produces retrograde for an outer planet
Indicate when Mars would appear brightest and opposite the Sun during the event
Complete a short explanation tying together observation from Earth and heliocentric cause
